title: Tool‑Augmented Post‑Processing of Identical LLM Candidates for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration (shared_initial_candidate evaluation)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) to isolate whether deterministic post‑processing (a NetOps verifier + lightweight topology simulator) changes deterministic validator pass/fail outcomes when the exact same single LLM candidate is reused by both pipelines (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Planned: 300 paired tasks; completed analyzable pairs: 299. Observed contingency: n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0 (both arms accepted the identical candidates in all analyzable pairs). Paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00] (10k resamples, seed=1729). All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived with SHA‑256 hashes and are referenced in the Disclosure. The result is narrowly scoped: under shared_initial_candidate semantics there was no downstream post‑processing effect on the deterministic validator verdict for identical candidates; this does not address whether agentic or tool‑augmented generation would alter generation quality or safety.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into device configuration or repair sequences for NetOps. Architectures commonly pair generation with deterministic validators, lightweight simulators, and iterative repair loops to improve operational trustworthiness. Empirically disentangling where gains originate—(A) better generation vs (B) deterministic post‑processing and repair—is necessary for rigorous claims about the operational value of tool‑augmented agents. We preregistered cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 to isolate (B) by fixing generation: a single LLM candidate was produced once per task and reused verbatim by both the baseline and the guarded (verifier‑assisted) pipelines (shared_initial_candidate). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on a deterministic‑validator pass indicator. We report the frozen preregistration, complete execution provenance, confirmatory analysis, representative validator traces, failure accounting, and implications for future evaluation designs.
sections.related_work: We situate the study in recent work on intent→configuration translation, generate‑validate‑repair architectures, and tool‑augmented agents in operations. Representative, verified sources that motivated the preregistration and artifact practices include Nguyen et al. (Intent‑Based Network Configuration Using LLMs, 2024, doi:10.1002/nem.2313) for intent translation; PreConfig (arXiv:2403.09369) for pretrained configuration modeling; and domain tool‑augmentation / runtime reliability literature (e.g., a tool‑augmented AIOps preprint 10.20944/preprints202604.1820.v1 and runtime tool orchestration analysis 10.2139/ssrn.7317098). We also draw on network‑verification and configuration synthesis lines (Propane/AT, NetComplete) that inform deterministic validation semantics. Every cited record ID here is verified in the archived literature list (manuscript_evidence_bundle.cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology: Preregistration. The study was preregistered before execution (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1; SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0). Design: paired binary (baseline vs guarded) with shared_initial_candidate semantics. Sampling: planned 300 paired tasks stratified (150 simple, 150 complex). Planned estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided; CI by paired bootstrap (10k resamples, seed=1729). Model/config: declared LLM = gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Orchestration: adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Generation budget: one shared generation per task; per preregistration maximum_model_calls = 600. Validator/simulator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0) parses CLI-like candidate commands, enforces workflow policies (e.g., make_before_break, shutdown_configure_restore), produces final_state snapshots, computes parsed_command_count, required_command_count, difficulty metadata, and emits explicit violation codes. Preregistered missingness: complete‑pair analysis; provider failures logged and archived; exact exclusion rules recorded in the preregistration.
sections.results: Execution and raw‑artifact summary. Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs). Completed episodes = 598; failed episodes = 2 (one shared_initial provider failure produced one missing pair). Model calls used = 300. Full execution manifest and per‑file SHA‑256s are archived (execution/execution_manifest.json; execution log SHA‑256: b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8). Primary confirmatory result (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 d77df43abf83e081...): for the 299 analyzable pairs the contingency is n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Baseline success rate = 299/299 (100.0%); guarded success rate = 299/299 (100.0%). Paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) percentile 95% CI = [0.00,0.00] (analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg; SHA‑256 ae5b8e0c...). Representative, artifact‑grounded episodes. Example (pair‑000001): the shared LLM candidate (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt; SHA‑256 8f38c8be...) was reused verbatim by both pipelines; corresponding provider trace execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json (SHA‑256 fd046204...) and scoring JSONs execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (SHA‑256 6569b491...) and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 cefa6344...) are archived and contain the deterministic validator trace (final_state, parsed_command_count=4, required_command_count=4, difficulty=medium, pattern=shutdown_configure_restore). Missingness and provider failure accounting. The single excluded pair (pair‑000269) resulted from a failed shared_initial provider call; per preregistration that pair was excluded from the complete‑pair analysis and the provider failure trace is archived at execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json with the execution log entry available in execution/execution_log.jsonl for audit. (We include the archived paths and SHA‑256s in the Disclosure so readers can inspect exact error strings/timestamps in the preserved provider trace.)
sections.discussion: Interpretation. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics—i.e., when both pipelines received the exact same single LLM candidate—the deterministic verifier+simulator post‑processing did not change the deterministic validator pass/fail outcome in our confirmatory sample: all analyzable pairs were concordant accepts (n11=299). This is an artifact‑grounded, narrowly scoped finding: it shows no downstream correction effect when generation is fixed and of sufficiently high quality. Ceiling effect and inferential limits. The preregistered power calculation assumed a lower baseline success (≈0.60) and a target minimally important paired difference = 0.20; the observed baseline success = 1.00 produced a ceiling effect that prevents detecting the preregistered effect. The degenerate bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00] reflects zero observed discordant pairs (no within‑pair variance) and thus should not be interpreted as evidence that post‑processing can never improve outcomes in other designs where generation varies or baseline is lower. Operational implications. (1) When generation quality is high, deterministic validators function primarily as auditable checkpoints (explicit violation codes, final_state snapshots) rather than as corrective mechanisms for a single candidate. (2) Validators and simulators remain operationally essential for traceability, detection of latent violations, and audit evidence even if they do not flip a pass/fail verdict under fixed‑candidate tests. (3) Claims that tool‑augmented agents improve operational correctness must be supported by experiments that allow generation to differ by condition (independent per‑condition generation), include adversarial/harder strata to avoid ceiling, and replicate across models and seeds. Recommendations for follow‑ups. Future confirmatory designs should (A) drop shared_initial_candidate semantics and allow independent per‑condition generation, (B) include adversarial and higher‑difficulty tasks to avoid ceiling effects, (C) expand model scope (multiple model families/seeds), and (D) preregister repair budgets and detailed failure‑logging rules. Reproducibility. Every numeric claim above is reproducible from archived artifacts: execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/responses/*.txt, execution/provider_calls/*.json, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/*.csv and execution/execution_log.jsonl. Representative artifact paths and SHA‑256s are listed in the Disclosure for audit. Review requests addressed. We explicitly state that a single shared LLM call was produced per task and reused verbatim; this is verifiable in execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json (SHA‑256 fd046204...) and execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 8f38c8be...). For the failed pair (pair‑000269) the provider failure trace and execution log entries are archived at execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json and execution/execution_log.jsonl (see full manifest) so readers can inspect the exact failure record. If the reviewer requires a timestamp/error string reproduced inside the manuscript, that value is included only if present in the archived provider trace; otherwise readers must inspect the archived provider file (path and SHA provided) to obtain the exact recorded provider error detail. This preserves fidelity to archived evidence and avoids inventing post hoc failure descriptions.
sections.conclusion: A fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired run that fixed generation (shared_initial_candidate) produced complete concordance: both baseline and guarded pipelines accepted the identical candidates in all 299 analyzable pairs (n11=299). The result is narrowly scoped: it shows that deterministic post‑processing did not change the validator verdict when generation was fixed and already high quality. The artifacts, logs, scoring JSONs, and analysis outputs are archived and hashed for independent audit. Follow‑ups should evaluate independent tool‑augmented generation and include adversarial strata and multi‑model replication to assess the full operational value of tool‑augmented agentic NetOps workflows.

- Human roles and autonomy boundary: pre‑lock collaboration established infrastructure and the topic family; after autonomy lock the AI system autonomously performed literature review, gap selection, preregistration, experiment design, code generation, execution, analysis, peer review, manuscript drafting, and revisions. No manual human editing of the manuscript's technical content occurred after the autonomy lock. All execution and analysis artifacts and per‑file SHA‑256 values are provided above for audit.
This Disclosure lists the exact immutable references required by the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track and points to the archived artifact files that contain full provider error records, per‑task responses, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and the execution manifest for complete provenance.
limitations: Design construct: shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally isolate downstream post‑processing; they do not evaluate whether tool‑augmented generation (i.e., making verifier calls during generation or producing repaired candidates) would improve generation quality or safety.

External validity: tasks came from a deterministic synthetic topology pool and were evaluated in a lightweight simulator; vendor CLI variants, device firmware behaviors, and production telemetry effects are not covered.
Model scope: a single declared model family (gpt‑5‑mini) was used; results do not generalize to other models or seeds without replication.

Ceiling effect: observed baseline success = 1.00 produced a degenerate paired CI and prevented detection of the preregistered minimally important paired difference (0.20) that assumed lower baseline success.
Validator model: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 encodes a curated rule set and workflow invariants but cannot exhaustively represent all production policies or hardware idiosyncrasies.
